name: Yara Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and your answers are confidential. What fills a normal site day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a formwork gang setting timber moulds and supports before concrete is poured on a car park. My trade certificate started me off, and years of deck work taught me where wet plywood and a bad prop can ruin a pour. A clean edge after stripping still feels good.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Raymond, my partner, does seasonal garden work, and our grown children live on their own. We have about four months saved and I earn the usual crew-lead rate, with some other sites nearby. My knees dislike cold decks, and I have never used AI tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the formwork gang that a quicker office note does not make concrete hold a shape by itself. We still have to brace the mould before anyone pours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Raymond and I have around four months of expenses saved, and my pay is normal for a crew lead. Our grown children live away, so we can keep working toward a retirement date if my knees and our accounts allow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would lead the car-park deck pour as planned and check the ties and props by hand. I would keep our usual monthly saving amount, without buying any AI tool I have never needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Cold plywood makes my knees ache, but my present wages look steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What check matters before the pour?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every prop needs a sound footing and every tie needs the correct spacing. A little leak in a concrete mould can turn into a costly rework.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you let an apprentice use AI for the checks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They can read what the office sends, but I want them to walk the deck and point to each prop. I have never used AI myself.

say: I would tell the crew **formwork props** still need a person checking them before concrete arrives.
I would accept modest **office time savings** without changing our site method.
think: Our **four-month cushion** and current wages make the next working years manageable.
My **knees** may decide retirement timing more than a small AI tool.
do: Keep leading **car-park formwork** and check ties and props by hand.
Maintain the existing **monthly saving amount** from wages.
feel: **Calm** about income, with ordinary pain from cold site work.
S0.quote: A little leak in a concrete mould can turn into a costly rework.
fieldNote: She has a moderate reserve, ordinary pay and **some nearby sites**.
Her refusal of AI fits the profile and preserves a **hands-on safety check** before each pour.

steps.text: Keep leading car-park formwork and checking props before pours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AI can buy timber and book concrete, but a screen cannot see a loose prop on a wet deck. I would ask the manager for a named carpenter on every computer-made pour plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Faster planning might shorten the gaps between jobs, or it might cut the paid time we use to set formwork safely. My own hours could shrink if the contractor prices each deck more tightly, and Raymond’s garden work is seasonal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare two rosters with my pay slips and tell the manager which setup hours disappeared. If they fall, Raymond and I would postpone replacing the garden fence until the next contract is confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about paid setup time. Four months of savings is useful, but a smaller wage still changes the plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who should sign the pour plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A carpenter who has walked the deck and checked the props. A name on the pour sheet means someone has to stand behind the measurement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the fence first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fence still stands. We would keep the savings for bills rather than spend it on timber while my paid hours are uncertain.

say: I would demand a **named carpenter** on every AI pour plan.
I would keep **prop checks** in the paid setup time before concrete is booked.
think: Tighter pricing could remove **paid setup hours** from my work.
Raymond’s **seasonal garden pay** would not fully replace a long cut.
do: Compare two **rosters and pay slips** for missing setup hours.
Delay the **garden fence** if paid hours fall until the next contract is confirmed.
feel: **Anxious** about a plausible reduction in her own pay.
S1.quote: A name on the pour sheet means someone has to stand behind the measurement.
fieldNote: Her worry concerns real **paid setup hours**, not an immediate robot pour.
The fence delay depends on **lost hours** and the next contract, preserving savings for bills.

steps.text: Delay garden fence only if setup pay falls before next contract is confirmed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the gang thinking AI in 2028 may plan the concrete, but a robot will not build the mould until around 2031. A first test should be on an empty site with power isolated while we mark the danger area.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty three when capable robots arrive. Raymond and I had hoped I could stop heavy work later, if the accounts and knees allow, so a cut to formwork days before then would affect our living.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep taking paid pours and ask the contractor for written crew plans. If two rosters cut my paid days, I would apply to posted nearby shuttering jobs only for a firm wage covering our household costs; I would leave only after an offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I have some savings and local options, but I do not want to lose the last earning years by surprise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire at the first robot test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Our retirement date is still a household calculation. A robot test is not an income plan for my household. I will work while the shifts and my knees allow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would safe testing look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Power off before a worker steps inside the marked area, then a qualified operator restarts the robot without anyone under a moving panel. I would stop the trial at the first missed command.

say: Thinking AI in **2028** plans pours before 2031 robots can build formwork.
I would require **isolated empty-site testing** before workers stand near a moving panel.
think: A cut to **paid formwork days** could arrive before retirement is affordable.
Our **four-month reserve** and some nearby sites give room to search.
do: Keep **paid pour shifts** while the contractor offers them.
Apply to **posted nearby shuttering roles** after two reduced rosters only for firm household-covering pay.
feel: **Anxious** about losing late-career wages, while retaining options.
S2.quote: A robot test is not an income plan for my household.
fieldNote: She treats retirement as an **affordability question**, not an automatic age-based exit.
Applications retain the **two-roster trigger**, posted local vacancy and firm household wage condition.

steps.text: Keep paid formwork pours while contractor shifts exist
Apply to posted nearby shuttering roles after two reduced rosters for firm household-covering pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years gives us time to test a robot on an awkward deck instead of a spotless demonstration. I would ask to see the stop switch work before concrete is booked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AI in 2031 might change the job sheets, while formwork robots arrive around 2034. I would be sixty six then and may have left the heavy site work if Raymond and I can afford it; I cannot promise that today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading pours next year and ask whether the contractor has a paid quality-check role. If a posted vacancy with funded training and paid study hours appears at a wage covering our bills, I would consider taking the course and applying; otherwise I would keep the current trade work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the work changing, calmer about my own pay over the next few years. I would rather know the numbers before making an exit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you join a trial if invited?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if it is an offered paid place, with the robot isolated before I enter the test area. Asking to see robot trial results is not the same as being on the trial crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would this card bring retirement forward?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. We would use actual savings and health to choose the date. A later robot does not pay for an earlier stop.

say: I would ask for **awkward-deck trials** before 2034 formwork robots spread.
I would check **stop controls** before anyone books a concrete pour.
think: I might leave heavy site work before **2034** if accounts and health permit.
The **2031 paperwork change** is smaller than the later physical robot work.
do: Keep leading **paid pours** next year while shifts continue.
Consider **funded quality training** only for a posted bill-covering role with paid study hours.
feel: **Uneasy** about later work while near-term income remains likely secure.
S3.quote: Asking to see robot trial results is not the same as being on the trial crew.
fieldNote: She makes a **trial request**, with participation conditional on an offered paid place.
Training is a future option only with **funding and paid time** for a posted role.

steps.text: Keep paid formwork pours next year while shifts continue
Review posted bill-covering quality roles with funded paid study before deciding whether to enrol

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now consider AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell apprentices they have years to learn formwork before thinking AI in 2036 and robots around 2039. I would still teach them to check props in the rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty eight at the thinking date and seventy one when robots follow. If Raymond and I can fund retirement before 2036, I expect to be off the heavy decks; if not, I would still need manageable paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading the 2026 pours and review our household figures with Raymond each winter. In the first year after 2036, if retired as planned I would stay off site; if still employed, I would take only ground-level paid checks my knees allow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about retirement funding, not the distant machine itself. A decade only helps if the money and the knees both hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop earlier because of this card?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. We have not fixed a guaranteed retirement date or payment. We will decide from actual expenses and my health.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What should an apprentice remember?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Check the prop footing after rain even if the drawing is clean. Wet ground can shift a load before a neat line on paper changes.

say: I would keep **prop checks** in apprenticeship before 2036 thinking AI and 2039 robots.
I would teach **wet-ground caution** during the long lead time.
think: Leaving the site before **2036** depends on affordable household figures.
If still working, I will need **manageable paid checks** rather than heavy lifts.
do: Keep **2026 pours** and review retirement accounts each winter.
After **2036**, take ground-level paid checks only if still employed and able.
feel: **Uneasy** about funding and health, with no near-term robot wage threat.
S4.quote: Wet ground can shift a load before a neat line on paper changes.
fieldNote: The 2026 work is definite; post-2036 shifts depend on **continued employment**.
She makes no **early-retirement claim** or assumption about a payment at a fixed age.

steps.text: Keep leading paid formwork pours during 2026 while knees allow
Take only ground-level paid checks after 2036 if still employed and knees allow

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable robots could cut paid formwork days by 2031 before Raymond and I know I can stop. A written crew plan, firm nearby work and safe isolated trials would help us decide.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who can halt a moving formwork robot when a worker is under the deck. A signed plan is no use after someone is hurt.

headlineQuote: A signed plan is no use after someone is hurt.
portrait: **Yara**, 58, is a skilled formwork lead with a trade certificate, typical pay, four months saved and some nearby construction work.
Raymond’s **seasonal garden income** helps, while her knees make heavy deck work harder as retirement approaches.
She avoids **AI tools**, trusts prop checks and will consider training only for a posted funded role with paid time.
The **2028 case** worries her because 2031 robots may reduce paid pours before retirement is affordable.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could reduce her paid formwork days before retirement is affordable.
whatWouldHelp: A written **crew plan**, firm nearby work and isolated safety trials would help.
